cards.explanation: The answer is True. Micah comes right out with it. He tells his mother, "…I have the silver here with me; I took it." (Judges 17:2) He had heard her utter a curse about that silver, and he owns up anyway. That's a man who walks up to the oven and says, "I'm the one who ate the dough."

The answer is "Blessed be my son by the LORD." That's what she says: "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) Picture it, friends. Her silver is gone, Micah says he heard her utter a curse about it, and then her own boy says he took it. I would have expected a very different speech.

The answer is a graven image and a molten idol. She says she wholly dedicates the silver to the LORD to make "…a graven image and a molten idol." (Judges 17:3) Those are the two things she names. I'll just say this plainly, friends: it's a heavy thing to see an image come out of silver she said was for the LORD.

The answer is house. The graven image and molten idol "…were placed in the house of Micah." (Judges 17:4) Two hundred shekels of silver went to a silversmith, and the finished pieces ended up under Micah's roof. That's quite a trip for some silver, friends.

The answer is sons. Micah "…ordained one of his sons as his priest." (Judges 17:5) He keeps the priest job inside his own family. The verse says he had a shrine and made an ephod and some household idols, and then he picked a son for the job.

The answer is that each person decides for himself. The writer says, "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." (Judges 17:6) With no king, nobody is named as the one who decides for everybody. Picture a bakery with no head baker and everyone writing their own recipe, friends.

The answer is False. The young Levite "…left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle where he could find a place." (Judges 17:8) The text gives his own reason for leaving, and it isn't a message from Micah. He came to Micah's house as he traveled.

The answer is ten shekels a year plus clothes and provisions. That's the offer: "…ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions." (Judges 17:10) Micah asks him to "…be my father and priest…" Ten silver shekels, a suit and his provisions, and the young man goes in and agrees to stay.
The answer is son. "…the young man became like a son to Micah." (Judges 17:11) Micah had asked him to be his father and priest. Now the Levite is treated like family under that roof.

The answer is True. "Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house." (Judges 17:12) Earlier, Micah ordained one of his own sons. Now the Levite is the priest, and he's living right there in the house.

The answer is because a Levite has become his priest. Micah says, "Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest." (Judges 17:13) He's sure because of the Levite. I'll say it gently, friends: I think Micah is leaning hard on that one fact. And the story isn't over, so stay with me.
